_link.title: I can describe what a gravitational field is and why it is classified as a vector field

toLevel2.question: What is a gravitational field?
toLevel2.correct: A region of space where an object with mass experiences a gravitational force
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A gravitational field is defined as a region of space surrounding a mass in which any other mass will experience a gravitational force. The field exists at every point in the space around the mass.

distractors.answer: A force that acts between two objects in contact
distractors.explanation: A gravitational field is not a contact force. It is a region of space where a gravitational force acts at a distance, without requiring physical contact between the masses.

distractors.answer: The gravitational force exerted on an object at Earth's surface
distractors.explanation: The gravitational force at Earth's surface is a specific value of force at one location. A gravitational field is the entire region of space where a mass experiences a gravitational force.

distractors.answer: A measure of the mass of an object
distractors.explanation: Mass is a property of an object, not a field. A gravitational field is a region of space where any object with mass experiences a gravitational force.

toLevel2.question: Why is a gravitational field classified as a vector field?
toLevel2.correct: Because at every point it has both a magnitude and a direction
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A vector quantity has both magnitude and direction. The gravitational field at every point has a magnitude (the field strength, measured in N kg⁻¹) and a direction (toward the centre of the attracting mass), so it is a vector field.

distractors.explanation: A quantity with magnitude only is a scalar, not a vector. The gravitational field has both magnitude (field strength) and direction (toward the attracting mass), which makes it a vector field.

distractors.answer: Because it can only act in one direction
distractors.explanation: The gravitational field acts toward the centre of the attracting mass from all surrounding points, so its direction varies depending on position. It is a vector field because it has both magnitude and direction at every point.

distractors.answer: Because its strength is constant everywhere
distractors.explanation: The gravitational field strength is not constant — it varies with distance from the mass. It is classified as a vector field because at every point it has both magnitude and direction.

toLevel2.question: What are the two properties needed to fully describe the gravitational field at a point in space?
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Because the gravitational field is a vector field, it requires both a magnitude (the gravitational field strength, in N kg⁻¹) and a direction (toward the centre of the attracting mass) to be fully described at any point.

distractors.explanation: Mass and distance are used to calculate the field strength, but they do not describe the field at a point. The field at a point is described by its magnitude and direction.
Speed and acceleration describe motion, not a field. A gravitational field at a point is described by its magnitude (field strength) and direction.
Magnitude alone is insufficient because the gravitational field is a vector quantity. Both magnitude and direction are needed to fully describe the field at a point.

toLevel2.question: What is the SI unit of gravitational field strength?
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Gravitational field strength is defined as the gravitational force per unit mass (g = F/m), so its unit is newtons per kilogram (N kg⁻¹).

distractors.explanation: This is not a standard unit for any common physical quantity. The unit of gravitational field strength is N kg⁻¹, derived from force per unit mass.
J kg⁻¹ is the unit of gravitational potential (energy per unit mass), not gravitational field strength. The field strength has units of N kg⁻¹.
N m⁻² is the unit of pressure (pascals), not gravitational field strength. The field strength is measured in N kg⁻¹.

toLevel2.question: In which direction does the gravitational field of the Earth point?
toLevel2.correct: Toward the centre of the Earth
toLevel2.correctExplanation: The gravitational field is directed toward the centre of the mass that creates it. For Earth, the gravitational field at any point in the surrounding space is directed toward the centre of the Earth.

distractors.answer: Away from the centre of the Earth
distractors.explanation: The gravitational field is directed toward the centre of the attracting mass, not away from it. Gravity is an attractive force, so the field points inward.

distractors.answer: Tangent to the surface of the Earth
distractors.explanation: The gravitational field is directed radially inward toward the centre of the Earth, not tangentially along the surface.

distractors.answer: In the direction of the Earth's rotation
distractors.explanation: The gravitational field direction is determined by the mass distribution, not the rotation. It is directed toward the centre of the Earth.

toLevel2.prompt: Complete the definition of a gravitational field.
toLevel2.sentence: A gravitational field is a region of {{blank:1}} where an object with {{blank:2}} experiences a gravitational force.

1.correctExplanation: A gravitational field is defined as a region of space surrounding a mass where any other mass will experience a gravitational force.

distractors.explanation: A gravitational field exists in the space around a mass, not in matter itself. It is a region of space, not a region of matter.
A gravitational field is a region of space, not a region of energy. While energy is associated with the field, the field itself is defined as a region of space.

2.correctExplanation: The gravitational field exerts a force on any object that has mass. Mass is the property that determines whether an object interacts with a gravitational field.

distractors.explanation: Charge is the property relevant to electric fields, not gravitational fields. Gravitational fields act on objects with mass.
Velocity does not determine whether an object experiences a gravitational force. Any object with mass in a gravitational field experiences a gravitational force, regardless of its velocity.

toLevel2.prompt: Complete the sentence explaining why the gravitational field is a vector field.
toLevel2.sentence: The gravitational field is a vector field because at every point in space it has both a {{blank:1}} and a {{blank:2}}.

1.correctExplanation: A vector quantity requires both magnitude and direction. The magnitude of the gravitational field at a point is the gravitational field strength, measured in N kg⁻¹.

distractors.explanation: Mass is a property of an object, not a property of the field at a point. The gravitational field at a point is described by its magnitude (field strength) and direction.
Temperature is a scalar quantity unrelated to gravitational fields. The gravitational field at a point is described by its magnitude and direction.

2.correctExplanation: The direction of the gravitational field is toward the centre of the attracting mass. Together with the magnitude, the direction completes the vector description of the field at a point.

distractors.explanation: Frequency is not a property of a gravitational field. The two properties of a vector field at a point are magnitude and direction.
Wavelength is a property of waves, not gravitational fields. A vector field is defined by its magnitude and direction at every point.

toLevel2.prompt: Complete the sentence about the direction of a gravitational field.
toLevel2.sentence: The gravitational field at any point around a spherical mass is directed toward the {{blank:1}} of that mass.

1.correctExplanation: For a spherical mass, the gravitational field at any external point is directed radially inward toward the centre of the mass. This is because a uniform sphere behaves gravitationally as if all its mass were concentrated at its centre.

distractors.explanation: The gravitational field is directed toward the centre of the mass, not toward its surface. For a spherical mass, all field lines point radially inward toward the centre.
A sphere does not have an edge, and the gravitational field is directed toward the centre of the mass, not toward any particular part of its surface.

toLevel2.question: A gravitational field is a scalar field because it only has magnitude.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A gravitational field is a vector field, not a scalar field. At every point, the gravitational field has both a magnitude (field strength) and a direction (toward the centre of the attracting mass).

distractors.explanation: The gravitational field has both magnitude and direction at every point, making it a vector field. A scalar field, such as temperature, has magnitude only.

toLevel2.question: The gravitational field exists in the space surrounding a mass, even when no other object is present to experience the force.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: The gravitational field is a property of the space around a mass. It exists regardless of whether a second mass is present to experience the force. If a mass were placed at any point in the field, it would experience a gravitational force.

distractors.explanation: The gravitational field exists independently of whether another mass is present. The field is created by the mass and exists in the surrounding space at all times.

toLevel3.question: Which of the following best explains the difference between a vector field and a scalar field?
toLevel3.correct: A vector field has both magnitude and direction at every point, while a scalar field has magnitude only
toLevel3.correctExplanation: A vector field assigns a vector (with magnitude and direction) to every point in space. A scalar field assigns only a scalar (magnitude) to every point. The gravitational field is a vector field; temperature is an example of a scalar field.

distractors.answer: A vector field has direction only, while a scalar field has magnitude only
distractors.explanation: A vector field has both magnitude and direction, not direction alone. A vector without magnitude would not be physically meaningful.

distractors.answer: A vector field is always uniform, while a scalar field varies with position
distractors.explanation: Both vector and scalar fields can be uniform or non-uniform. The distinction is that a vector field has magnitude and direction, while a scalar field has magnitude only.

distractors.answer: A vector field acts only at the surface of an object, while a scalar field fills all of space
distractors.explanation: Both vector and scalar fields can exist throughout all of space. The distinction is about the type of quantity (vector vs scalar) at each point, not where the field exists.

toLevel3.question: At a point 1000 km above Earth's surface, the gravitational field strength is approximately 7.3 N kg⁻¹. Which of the following provides the most complete description of the gravitational field at this point?
toLevel3.correct: The field has a strength of 7.3 N kg⁻¹ directed toward the centre of the Earth
toLevel3.correctExplanation: A complete description of a vector field at a point requires both its magnitude and direction. The magnitude is 7.3 N kg⁻¹ and the direction is toward the centre of the Earth.

distractors.answer: The field has a strength of 7.3 N kg⁻¹
distractors.explanation: This provides only the magnitude. Since the gravitational field is a vector field, the direction (toward the centre of the Earth) must also be stated for a complete description.

distractors.answer: The field is directed toward the centre of the Earth
distractors.explanation: This provides only the direction. Since the gravitational field is a vector, the magnitude (7.3 N kg⁻¹) must also be stated for a complete description.

distractors.answer: The field is 7.3 N kg⁻¹ directed away from the Earth
distractors.explanation: The direction is incorrect. The gravitational field is directed toward the centre of the Earth, not away from it, because gravity is an attractive force.

toLevel3.question: Which of the following is an example of a scalar field?
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Temperature is a scalar quantity — at every point in the room it has a magnitude (a temperature value) but no direction. This makes the temperature distribution a scalar field.

distractors.answer: The gravitational field around the Earth
distractors.explanation: The gravitational field is a vector field because at every point it has both magnitude (field strength) and direction (toward the centre of the Earth).

distractors.answer: The electric field between two charged plates
distractors.explanation: The electric field is a vector field — at every point between the plates it has both magnitude and direction.

distractors.answer: The velocity field of flowing water
distractors.explanation: The velocity field of flowing water is a vector field because at every point the water velocity has both magnitude (speed) and direction.

toLevel3.question: Two students discuss the gravitational field. Student A says: 'The gravitational field at a point tells us the force on a 1 kg mass at that point.' Student B says: 'The gravitational field at a point has both size and direction.' Which student is correct?
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Student A correctly describes gravitational field strength as the force per unit mass (g = F/m, so F = mg gives the force on 1 kg as numerically equal to g). Student B correctly identifies the gravitational field as a vector quantity with both magnitude and direction.

distractors.explanation: Student B is also correct. The gravitational field is a vector field, meaning it has both magnitude (size) and direction at every point.
Student A is also correct. The gravitational field strength at a point equals the force on a unit mass: g = F/m, so for m = 1 kg, F = g numerically.
Both students are correct. Student A correctly describes the physical meaning of field strength, and Student B correctly identifies the field as a vector quantity.

toLevel3.question: An astronaut travels from Earth to the Moon. Which of the following best describes how the gravitational field of the Earth changes along this path?
toLevel3.correct: The magnitude decreases and the direction remains toward the centre of the Earth
toLevel3.correctExplanation: As the astronaut moves farther from Earth, the gravitational field strength decreases (it follows an inverse square relationship). The direction of Earth's field always points toward the centre of the Earth from any point in space.

distractors.answer: The magnitude stays constant and the direction remains toward the centre of the Earth
distractors.explanation: The magnitude of the gravitational field decreases with increasing distance from Earth (following an inverse square law). It is not constant.

distractors.answer: The magnitude decreases and the direction reverses halfway
distractors.explanation: The direction of Earth's gravitational field always points toward the centre of the Earth. It does not reverse. However, the Moon has its own gravitational field, and at some point the Moon's field may dominate.

distractors.answer: The magnitude increases and the direction remains toward the centre of the Earth
distractors.explanation: The gravitational field strength decreases with distance from Earth, not increases. The field is stronger closer to the mass.

toLevel3.question: What does it mean physically to say the gravitational field strength at a point is 9.8 N kg⁻¹?
toLevel3.correct: A mass of 1 kg placed at that point would experience a gravitational force of 9.8 N
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Gravitational field strength is defined as the gravitational force per unit mass: g = F/m. A field strength of 9.8 N kg⁻¹ means that every kilogram of mass at that point experiences a gravitational force of 9.8 N.

distractors.answer: A mass of 9.8 kg is present at that point
distractors.explanation: The field strength does not tell us the mass at the point. It tells us the force per unit mass: a 1 kg mass would experience 9.8 N of force.

distractors.answer: The gravitational force at that point is always 9.8 N regardless of the mass placed there
distractors.explanation: The force depends on the mass: F = mg. A field strength of 9.8 N kg⁻¹ means the force per kilogram is 9.8 N. A 2 kg mass would experience 19.6 N.

distractors.answer: The gravitational potential energy at that point is 9.8 J
distractors.explanation: Gravitational field strength (N kg⁻¹) is not the same as gravitational potential energy (measured in joules). It represents the force per unit mass at that point.

toLevel3.prompt: Complete the sentence about vector and scalar fields.
toLevel3.sentence: A gravitational field is a {{blank:1}} field because it has both magnitude and direction, unlike a {{blank:2}} field such as temperature which has magnitude only.

1.correctExplanation: The gravitational field assigns a vector (with magnitude and direction) to every point in space, making it a vector field.

distractors.explanation: A scalar field has magnitude only. The gravitational field has both magnitude and direction, so it is a vector field.
Uniform describes whether the field is the same at every point, not whether it is a vector or scalar. The gravitational field is a vector field because it has both magnitude and direction.

2.correctExplanation: Temperature is a scalar quantity (magnitude only, no direction), so a temperature distribution is a scalar field. This contrasts with a vector field like the gravitational field.

distractors.explanation: Temperature has magnitude only and no direction, making it a scalar field, not a vector field.
The gravitational field is a vector field, not a scalar field. Temperature is an example of a scalar field because it has magnitude only.

toLevel3.prompt: Complete the sentence about the gravitational field strength.
toLevel3.sentence: The gravitational field strength at a point is defined as the gravitational {{blank:1}} per unit {{blank:2}} at that point, and has units of N kg⁻¹.

1.correctExplanation: Gravitational field strength is defined as the gravitational force per unit mass: g = F/m. It tells us how much force a unit mass would experience at that point.

distractors.explanation: Gravitational energy per unit mass is gravitational potential, not field strength. The gravitational field strength is the gravitational force per unit mass.
While the field strength is numerically equal to the acceleration due to gravity, the definition is in terms of force per unit mass, not acceleration per unit mass.

2.correctExplanation: The gravitational field strength is force per unit mass (g = F/m), giving units of N kg⁻¹. This means it describes the force experienced by each kilogram of mass at that point.

distractors.explanation: Force per unit charge defines the electric field strength, not the gravitational field strength. Gravitational field strength is force per unit mass.
Force per unit distance is not a standard physical quantity. Gravitational field strength is force per unit mass, with units of N kg⁻¹.

toLevel3.prompt: Complete the sentence about what creates a gravitational field.
toLevel3.sentence: A gravitational field is created by any object that has {{blank:1}}. The field extends outward through the surrounding {{blank:2}} in all directions.

1.correctExplanation: Any object with mass creates a gravitational field in the space around it. The greater the mass, the stronger the gravitational field.

distractors.explanation: Charge creates an electric field, not a gravitational field. Gravitational fields are created by mass.
Velocity does not create a gravitational field. A gravitational field is created by an object with mass, regardless of whether it is moving.

2.correctExplanation: The gravitational field extends through the surrounding space in all directions from the mass. It is a property of the space around the mass.

distractors.explanation: The gravitational field extends through space, not just through matter. It exists in the vacuum of space as well as through material objects.
The gravitational field exists in all of space around a mass, not only in the atmosphere. It extends outward in all directions, including into the vacuum of space.

toLevel3.question: The direction of the gravitational field at a point near Earth's surface is vertically upward, away from the Earth.
toLevel3.correctExplanation: The gravitational field is directed toward the centre of the attracting mass. Near Earth's surface, this means the field is directed vertically downward, toward the centre of the Earth, not upward.

distractors.explanation: The gravitational field near Earth's surface is directed toward the centre of the Earth, which is vertically downward. The field is attractive, so it points toward the mass, not away from it.

toLevel4.question: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the gravitational field from the gravitational force?
toLevel4.correct: The gravitational field is a property of the space around a mass, while the gravitational force is the force exerted on a specific mass placed in the field
toLevel4.correctExplanation: The gravitational field exists at every point in space around a mass, regardless of whether another mass is present. The gravitational force is the specific force experienced by a particular mass placed in the field: F = mg.

distractors.answer: The gravitational field and the gravitational force are the same quantity expressed in different units
distractors.explanation: They are different quantities. The field (measured in N kg⁻¹) describes the field at a point per unit mass, while the force (measured in N) is the actual force on a specific mass.

distractors.answer: The gravitational force is a property of space, while the gravitational field depends on the mass of the object
distractors.explanation: This is the reverse of the correct relationship. The gravitational field is the property of space around a mass. The gravitational force depends on the mass of the object placed in the field.

distractors.answer: The gravitational field only exists when two masses are present, while the gravitational force exists for a single mass
distractors.explanation: The gravitational field exists around a single mass regardless of whether a second mass is present. The gravitational force on an object requires the object to be in a gravitational field.

toLevel4.question: The gravitational field strength at a point 6.4 × 10⁶ m from the centre of the Earth is 9.8 N kg⁻¹. A 10 kg mass is placed at this point. What is the gravitational force on the mass, and in what direction does it act?
toLevel4.correct: 98 N directed toward the centre of the Earth
toLevel4.correctExplanation: The gravitational force is F = mg = 10 × 9.8 = 98 N. Since the gravitational field is a vector field directed toward the centre of the Earth, the force on the mass also acts in this direction.

distractors.answer: 98 N directed away from the centre of the Earth
distractors.explanation: The direction is incorrect. The gravitational field (and therefore the force on the mass) is directed toward the centre of the Earth, not away from it.

distractors.answer: 9.8 N directed toward the centre of the Earth
distractors.explanation: This is the field strength (9.8 N kg⁻¹), not the force on a 10 kg mass. The force is F = mg = 10 × 9.8 = 98 N.

distractors.answer: 0.98 N directed toward the centre of the Earth
distractors.explanation: This would be the force on a 0.1 kg mass. For a 10 kg mass, F = mg = 10 × 9.8 = 98 N.

toLevel4.question: A student says: 'The gravitational field is a scalar because gravitational field strength is just a number like 9.8.' Which of the following is the best response?
toLevel4.correct: Gravitational field strength is not just a number — at every point it also has a direction toward the centre of the attracting mass, making it a vector field
toLevel4.correctExplanation: While the magnitude of the field strength can be expressed as a number, the field at every point also has a direction (toward the centre of the mass). Both magnitude and direction are needed, which makes it a vector field.

distractors.answer: The student is correct — gravitational field strength is a scalar because it is always positive
distractors.explanation: Being always positive does not make a quantity scalar. The gravitational field has both magnitude and direction at every point, making it a vector field. Vectors can have positive magnitudes while still being vectors.

distractors.answer: The student is correct because the gravitational field has no direction associated with it
distractors.explanation: The gravitational field does have a direction — it is directed toward the centre of the attracting mass. This direction is essential for solving force and motion problems.

distractors.answer: The gravitational field is a vector only when the field is non-uniform
distractors.explanation: The gravitational field is a vector field regardless of whether it is uniform or non-uniform. At every point it has both magnitude and direction.

toLevel4.question: At a particular point in space, two gravitational fields overlap: one from the Earth (directed to the left, 6.0 N kg⁻¹) and one from the Moon (directed to the right, 2.0 N kg⁻¹). What is the net gravitational field at that point?
toLevel4.correct: 4.0 N kg⁻¹ directed to the left
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Since gravitational fields are vector fields, they add as vectors. The two fields act in opposite directions, so the net field is 6.0 − 2.0 = 4.0 N kg⁻¹ in the direction of the stronger field (to the left, toward Earth).

distractors.answer: 8.0 N kg⁻¹ directed to the left
distractors.explanation: This would be the result if both fields pointed in the same direction. Since they point in opposite directions, the net field is the difference: 6.0 − 2.0 = 4.0 N kg⁻¹.

distractors.answer: 4.0 N kg⁻¹ directed to the right
distractors.explanation: The magnitude is correct (6.0 − 2.0 = 4.0 N kg⁻¹), but the direction is wrong. The net field is in the direction of the stronger field, which is to the left (toward Earth).

distractors.answer: 2.0 N kg⁻¹ directed to the right
distractors.explanation: This is just the Moon's field alone. The net field is the vector sum: 6.0 − 2.0 = 4.0 N kg⁻¹ in the direction of the stronger Earth field (to the left).

toLevel4.question: Which of the following explains why we need to know the direction of the gravitational field, not just its magnitude?
toLevel4.correct: The direction determines which way a mass will accelerate when placed in the field
toLevel4.correctExplanation: The gravitational field at a point determines the force on a mass placed there (F = mg), and the direction of this force determines the direction of the resulting acceleration. Without knowing the direction, we cannot predict the motion of objects.

distractors.answer: The magnitude alone is sufficient because gravity always acts downward
distractors.explanation: 'Downward' is only meaningful near a single spherical mass. In general, the gravitational field can point in any direction depending on the configuration of masses. The direction is essential.

distractors.answer: The direction is needed only for non-uniform fields
distractors.explanation: The direction is needed for both uniform and non-uniform fields. Even in a uniform field, the direction tells us which way the force acts.

distractors.answer: The direction is only relevant when calculating gravitational potential energy
distractors.explanation: The direction of the gravitational field is relevant whenever we need to determine the force on a mass, the acceleration of an object, or the trajectory of a projectile — not just for energy calculations.

toLevel4.question: A satellite orbits the Earth in a circular orbit. At a particular point in its orbit, the gravitational field has a magnitude of 8.5 N kg⁻¹. Which of the following correctly describes the direction of the field at this point?
toLevel4.correct: Directed from the satellite's position toward the centre of the Earth
toLevel4.correctExplanation: The gravitational field at any point is directed toward the centre of the mass creating the field. For Earth's gravitational field, this means the field at the satellite's position points from the satellite toward the centre of the Earth.

distractors.answer: Directed along the satellite's velocity (tangent to the orbit)
distractors.explanation: The gravitational field is directed toward the centre of the Earth (radially inward), not along the velocity of the satellite. The velocity is tangent to the orbit, which is perpendicular to the field direction.

distractors.answer: Directed from the centre of the Earth outward toward the satellite
distractors.explanation: The gravitational field is directed toward the centre of the attracting mass (the Earth), not away from it. Gravity is an attractive force.

distractors.answer: Directed perpendicular to the line joining the satellite and Earth's centre
distractors.explanation: The gravitational field is directed along the line joining the satellite to Earth's centre, pointing toward the centre of the Earth, not perpendicular to this line.

toLevel4.question: Which of the following physical quantities is a vector?
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Gravitational field strength has both magnitude (measured in N kg⁻¹) and direction (toward the centre of the attracting mass), making it a vector quantity.

distractors.explanation: Mass is a scalar quantity — it has magnitude only and no direction.
Gravitational potential energy is a scalar quantity — it has magnitude only (measured in joules) and no direction.
Temperature is a scalar quantity — it has magnitude only and no direction.

toLevel4.prompt: Complete the sentence about the vector nature of the gravitational field.
toLevel4.sentence: Because the gravitational field is a vector field, two overlapping fields must be added using {{blank:1}} addition, taking into account both their magnitudes and {{blank:2}}.

1.correctExplanation: Vector fields must be combined using vector addition, which accounts for both the magnitude and direction of each field. Simple arithmetic addition only works when the fields are in the same direction.

distractors.explanation: Scalar addition would ignore the direction of the fields. Since gravitational fields are vectors, they must be combined using vector addition.
While algebraic addition can apply in one dimension, the correct general term is vector addition, which accounts for both magnitude and direction in two or three dimensions.

2.correctExplanation: When adding vectors, both the magnitude and direction of each vector must be considered. Two fields in opposite directions partially cancel, while fields in the same direction reinforce.

distractors.explanation: Vector addition combines the field vectors themselves (magnitude and direction), not the masses. The masses determine each individual field, but the addition is of the field vectors.
While both fields must have the same units to be added, the key consideration in vector addition is the direction of each field, not its units.

toLevel4.prompt: Complete the sentence comparing the gravitational field and gravitational force.
toLevel4.sentence: The gravitational field strength at a point is independent of the {{blank:1}} of the object placed there, while the gravitational force on the object {{blank:2}} on its mass.

1.correctExplanation: The gravitational field strength at a point depends only on the mass creating the field and the distance from it. It does not depend on the mass of any object placed in the field. The force, however, does depend on the mass (F = mg).

distractors.explanation: The gravitational field strength does depend on position (it changes with distance from the source mass). It is independent of the mass of the object placed in the field.
The gravitational field strength is independent of both the velocity and the mass of the test object, but mass is the more relevant distinction when comparing field strength and gravitational force.

2.correctExplanation: The gravitational force on an object is F = mg, which directly depends on the mass of the object. A larger mass experiences a greater gravitational force in the same field.

distractors.explanation: The gravitational force does depend on the mass of the object: F = mg. It is the field strength, not the force, that is independent of the test mass.
The mass of the object directly affects the gravitational force: F = mg. Greater mass means greater force for the same field strength.

toLevel4.prompt: Complete the sentence about the gravitational field near Earth's surface.
toLevel4.sentence: Near Earth's surface, the gravitational field strength is approximately {{blank:1}} N kg⁻¹ directed {{blank:2}}.

1.correctExplanation: The gravitational field strength at Earth's surface is approximately 9.8 N kg⁻¹. This means a 1 kg mass at Earth's surface experiences a gravitational force of approximately 9.8 N.

distractors.explanation: The value 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ is the universal gravitational constant G, not the field strength at Earth's surface. The surface field strength is approximately 9.8 N kg⁻¹.
The value 3.7 N kg⁻¹ is approximately the gravitational field strength at the surface of Mars, not Earth. Earth's surface field strength is approximately 9.8 N kg⁻¹.

2.correct: toward the centre of the Earth
2.correctExplanation: The gravitational field is always directed toward the centre of the attracting mass. Near Earth's surface, this means the field points vertically downward, toward the centre of the Earth.

distractors.answer: away from the centre of the Earth
distractors.explanation: The gravitational field is directed toward the centre of the Earth, not away from it. Gravity is an attractive force.

distractors.answer: tangent to the surface of the Earth
distractors.explanation: The gravitational field is directed radially inward toward the centre of the Earth, not tangentially along the surface.

toLevel5.question: A 5.0 kg mass is located at a point where the gravitational fields of two planets overlap. Planet X contributes a field of 4.0 N kg⁻¹ directed to the north, and Planet Y contributes a field of 3.0 N kg⁻¹ directed to the east. What is the magnitude of the net gravitational force on the mass?
toLevel5.correctExplanation: The net field is found using Pythagoras: g_net = √(4.0² + 3.0²) = √(16 + 9) = √25 = 5.0 N kg⁻¹. The net force is F = mg_net = 5.0 × 5.0 = 25 N.

distractors.explanation: This would be the force if the fields were simply added arithmetically: (4.0 + 3.0) × 5.0 = 35 N. Since the fields are perpendicular, the net field must be found using vector addition (Pythagoras): g_net = 5.0 N kg⁻¹, giving F = 25 N.
This is the net field strength (5.0 N kg⁻¹), not the net force on the mass. The force is F = mg = 5.0 × 5.0 = 25 N.
This would be the force from only the 4.0 N kg⁻¹ field (5.0 × 4.0 = 20 N). The contribution from both fields must be included using vector addition.

toLevel5.question: At a point between the Earth and the Moon, the gravitational field due to the Earth has a magnitude of 3.3 × 10⁻³ N kg⁻¹ directed toward the Earth, and the field due to the Moon has a magnitude of 3.3 × 10⁻³ N kg⁻¹ directed toward the Moon. What is the net gravitational field at this point?
toLevel5.correctExplanation: The two fields are equal in magnitude but directed in opposite directions (one toward Earth, one toward Moon, along the same line). When added as vectors, they cancel completely, giving a net field of zero.

distractors.answer: 6.6 × 10⁻³ N kg⁻¹ directed toward the Earth
distractors.explanation: This would be the result if both fields pointed in the same direction. Since they point in opposite directions (toward different bodies), they cancel: 3.3 × 10⁻³ − 3.3 × 10⁻³ = 0.

distractors.answer: 3.3 × 10⁻³ N kg⁻¹ directed toward the Earth
distractors.explanation: This is the field due to Earth alone. When the Moon's field (equal in magnitude, opposite in direction) is added, the net field is zero.

distractors.answer: 6.6 × 10⁻³ N kg⁻¹ directed toward the Moon
distractors.explanation: This would require both fields to point toward the Moon, which is not the case. Earth's field points toward Earth. The two equal and opposite fields cancel to give zero.

toLevel5.question: A student claims that because gravitational field strength and acceleration due to gravity have the same numerical value and units, they are the same physical concept. Which of the following best evaluates this claim?
toLevel5.correct: They are numerically equivalent and can be used interchangeably in calculations, but conceptually the field strength describes a property of space while the acceleration describes the motion of an object
toLevel5.correctExplanation: While g = 9.8 N kg⁻¹ and g = 9.8 m s⁻² are numerically identical (since N kg⁻¹ = m s⁻²), they describe different things. The field strength is a property of the field at a point (exists whether or not an object is there), while the acceleration is the result of placing a mass in the field.

distractors.answer: The student is completely wrong — they have different numerical values
distractors.explanation: The numerical values are in fact the same (9.8 N kg⁻¹ = 9.8 m s⁻²). The distinction is conceptual: field strength is a property of space, while acceleration describes an object's motion.

distractors.answer: They are identical in every way and there is no conceptual distinction
distractors.explanation: While they are numerically the same, there is an important conceptual distinction. The gravitational field strength exists as a property of space regardless of whether a mass is present, while the acceleration requires an object to be meaningful.

distractors.answer: The gravitational field strength is always larger than the acceleration due to gravity
distractors.explanation: They have the same numerical value (N kg⁻¹ is equivalent to m s⁻²). The distinction is conceptual, not numerical.

toLevel5.question: Three identical masses are arranged at the corners of an equilateral triangle. Which of the following best describes the gravitational field at the centre of the triangle?
toLevel5.correct: Zero, because the three equal field contributions cancel by symmetry
toLevel5.correctExplanation: By symmetry, each mass contributes a field of equal magnitude directed from the centre toward that mass. The three vectors are separated by 120° and have equal magnitudes, so their vector sum is zero.

distractors.answer: Non-zero, directed toward one of the masses
distractors.explanation: Because all three masses are identical and equidistant from the centre, there is no preferred direction. The three field contributions are symmetric and cancel to give zero net field.

distractors.answer: Non-zero, directed outward from the centre of the triangle
distractors.explanation: Gravitational fields are directed toward masses, not away from them. Moreover, the three equal contributions from each mass cancel by symmetry at the centre.

distractors.answer: Three times the field of a single mass, because the contributions add
distractors.explanation: The fields do not simply add arithmetically because they point in different directions (separated by 120°). When combined as vectors, they cancel to give zero net field at the centre.

toLevel5.question: The gravitational field strength at a distance r from a planet is g. A probe is placed at this point. Later, the probe's mass is doubled. What is the gravitational field strength at the same point?
toLevel5.correctExplanation: The gravitational field strength at a point depends only on the mass of the body creating the field and the distance from it. It is independent of the mass of any object placed in the field. Doubling the probe's mass does not change the field strength.

distractors.explanation: The field strength does not change when the mass of the test object changes. The field is a property of the space around the planet. The gravitational force on the probe would double (F = mg), but the field strength remains g.
The field strength is independent of the mass of the probe. Changing the probe's mass does not affect the field. Only the force on the probe changes (F = mg).
The field strength does not change with the mass of the test object. It remains g regardless of the probe's mass.

toLevel5.question: A deep space probe is at a point where the gravitational fields from two distant stars overlap. Star A produces a field of 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ N kg⁻¹ directed north, and Star B produces a field of 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ N kg⁻¹ directed east. What is the direction of the net gravitational field at the probe's location?
toLevel5.correctExplanation: The two perpendicular fields have equal magnitudes. Using vector addition, the resultant is directed at 45° between the two component directions, which is northeast. The angle is tan⁻¹(2.0/2.0) = 45° from north toward east.

distractors.explanation: If only Star A's field were present, the net field would be north. With Star B's field directed east, the resultant is the vector sum of both, pointing northeast.
If only Star B's field were present, the net field would be east. The vector sum of the northward and eastward fields gives a resultant directed northeast.
Star B's field is directed east, not west. The vector sum of a northward and an eastward field points northeast, not northwest.

toLevel5.question: A student draws a diagram showing gravitational field vectors at several points around the Earth. Which of the following would be correct features of this diagram?
toLevel5.correct: All vectors point toward the centre of the Earth, with longer arrows closer to the surface
toLevel5.correctExplanation: The gravitational field at any point is directed toward the centre of the Earth. The field strength decreases with distance from the centre (inverse square law), so vectors closer to the surface should be longer (representing stronger field).

distractors.answer: All vectors point away from the centre of the Earth, with longer arrows closer to the surface
distractors.explanation: The direction is incorrect. The gravitational field is directed toward the centre of the Earth (gravity is attractive), not away from it.

distractors.answer: All vectors point toward the centre of the Earth, with equal lengths at all distances
distractors.explanation: While the direction is correct, the lengths should vary. The gravitational field strength decreases with distance from the Earth, so vectors farther from the surface should be shorter.

distractors.answer: All vectors point toward the centre of the Earth, with longer arrows farther from the surface
distractors.explanation: The direction is correct, but the lengths should be longer closer to the surface, not farther away. Gravitational field strength decreases with distance.

toLevel5.question: Which of the following is the most accurate statement about why the gravitational field is described as a vector field rather than a scalar field?
toLevel5.correct: At every point in space the field has a specific magnitude and a specific direction, and both are required to determine the force on a mass
toLevel5.correctExplanation: A vector field is one where each point in space is assigned a vector quantity — one with both magnitude and direction. The gravitational field satisfies this because the field strength and its direction toward the attracting mass are both needed to find the force (F = mg, in the direction of g).

distractors.answer: The gravitational field has units of N kg⁻¹, and any quantity with these units is a vector
distractors.explanation: The units alone do not determine whether a quantity is a vector or scalar. The gravitational field is a vector because it has both magnitude and direction at every point.

distractors.answer: The gravitational field can be positive or negative, which makes it a vector
distractors.explanation: Having positive or negative values does not make a quantity a vector (temperature can be positive or negative but is scalar). The gravitational field is a vector because it has both magnitude and direction.

distractors.answer: All fields in physics are vector fields
distractors.explanation: Not all fields are vector fields. Temperature fields and gravitational potential fields are scalar fields. The gravitational field is specifically a vector field because it has both magnitude and direction.

toLevel5.prompt: Complete the sentence about the vector addition of gravitational fields.
toLevel5.sentence: When two gravitational fields of equal magnitude act at right angles to each other at a point, the magnitude of the net field is found using {{blank:1}} theorem, giving a net field that is {{blank:2}} times the individual field strength.

1.correctExplanation: When two perpendicular vectors of equal magnitude g are added, the resultant magnitude is √(g² + g²) = g√2. This uses Pythagoras' theorem for the right-angled triangle formed by the two field vectors.

distractors.explanation: Newton's laws relate force and motion. For adding perpendicular vectors, we use Pythagoras' theorem: the resultant of two perpendicular equal fields is √(g² + g²) = g√2.
Kepler's laws describe planetary motion, not vector addition. For perpendicular vector addition, Pythagoras' theorem gives the resultant magnitude.

2.correctExplanation: For two equal perpendicular field vectors of magnitude g, the resultant is √(g² + g²) = √(2g²) = g√2. So the net field is √2 (approximately 1.41) times the individual field strength.

distractors.explanation: The net field would be 2g only if the two fields pointed in the same direction. For perpendicular fields, the resultant is g√2 ≈ 1.41g, not 2g.
The net field would be zero only if the two equal fields pointed in opposite directions. For perpendicular fields, they do not cancel; the resultant is g√2.

toLevel5.prompt: Complete the sentence about the gravitational field at a point between two masses.
toLevel5.sentence: At a point directly between two unequal masses along the line joining them, the net gravitational field is the {{blank:1}} of the two individual fields because they point in {{blank:2}} directions.

1.correctExplanation: At a point between two masses, the gravitational field from each mass points toward that mass — and these directions are opposite. The net field is the difference of the two magnitudes, directed toward the more massive (or closer) body.

distractors.explanation: The fields point in opposite directions at a point between the two masses (each toward its own mass). Opposite vectors do not add; they subtract. The net field is the difference.
Vector fields are not multiplied when superposed — they are added as vectors. Since the fields point in opposite directions, the net field is the difference of their magnitudes.

2.correctExplanation: At a point between two masses, the gravitational field from one mass points to the left and the field from the other points to the right. These are opposite directions, so the fields partially cancel.

distractors.explanation: The fields do not point in the same direction at a point between the two masses. Each field points toward its source mass, which means they point in opposite directions.
At a point on the line joining the two masses, the fields from each mass are along this line but pointing in opposite directions toward their respective masses, not perpendicular.
